latin: Ex ista conclusione et conclusione paradoxa dogmatizante .xlvii. sequitur quod magia sit nobilissima pars scientiae naturalis.
latin_note: Copy-text Farmer 1998 (farmer1998:25125-25126), after the Rome print of 7 December 1486 (colophon farmer1998:28040-28042); Farmer's OCR 'conclusione_et' is read 'conclusione et'. The numeral '.xlvii.' is the reading of the print; the principle cited is 3>46 in the final text, so the reference is one out (farmer1998:25175-25176). Mandosio prints 'paradoxica' and marks the numeral '[sic]' (mandosio2012:564-565).
translation: It follows from the preceding conclusion and from paradoxical conclusion forty-seven, of those introducing new doctrine, that of natural science magic is the noblest part.
translation_note: 'conclusio paradoxa dogmatizans' refers to the section of 'paradoxical conclusions introducing new doctrines into philosophy', 3>1-71 (farmer1998:23418-23419). 'ex ista conclusione' is 9>3 (farmer1998:25175). The numeral is kept as printed; Copenhaver's translation silently gives 'number 46' (copenhaver2019:20288-20289).
translator: machine-drafted 2026-09-25 (agent WRITER-B2), from the Latin, checked against the sense of Farmer's English at farmer1998:25165; awaiting human check
attribution: Pico's own opinion: the fourth magical conclusion, a corollary drawn from 9>3 and a thesis of section 3> (farmer1998:25125-25126).

sources.text: Thesis 3>46: 'Dato quocunque obiecto practicabili, nobilior est operatio quae eum practicat quam quae eum contemplatur, si caetera sint paria'
sources.pico_relation: the major premise, cited by number

doctrine: The thesis is a syllogism stated in one sentence: magic is the practical part of natural science (9>3), and of any practicable object the operation that acts on it is nobler than the one that contemplates it, other things being equal (3>46); so magic is the noblest part of natural science (farmer1998:25122-25126; farmer1998:20976-20977). Farmer reads the pair 9>3-4 as claiming that it is 'our obligation to operate magic in the world' (farmer1998:25178-25179). Taken together, he writes, these theses seem not only to condone but to require us to work magic in the world (farmer1998:7262-7263). The operation required is not the mastery of nature: the magus as Pico pictured him was not a transformer of nature but its minister, ruled by the lowest order of angels and entrusted in turn with governing the material world (farmer1998:7272-7276). The Oration uses the same image of the magus as 'Nature's minister, not her Artificer', ascribed to Plotinus (copenhaver2019:19627-19628). Copenhaver reads the nobility by the height of the object: because magic and Kabbalah look to the stars and beyond, knowledge of them is nobler than the physics of change below the Moon (copenhaver2019:17648-17653).
context: The cross-reference is faulty: the thesis cited as the forty-seventh paradoxical dogmatizing conclusion is the forty-sixth in the printed text, which Farmer takes as evidence that one thesis was dropped from that section at a late date (farmer1998:25175-25178). In his note on the editio princeps Farmer argues that at least two theological theses and one from 3>1-71 were excluded while the work was in press, and he cites 9>4 as an example of the faulty cross-referencing (farmer1998:23416-23421). Pico's own copy of the text was numbered even though the printed edition was not, as cross-references like this one show (farmer1998:2133-2135). For Pico natural philosophy, of which magic was the apex and summit, was the third of four preparatory studies leading to the mystical ascent (farmer1998:7220-7223).
reception: In the Apology Pico repeated the claim, calling magic, in Mandosio's rendering, 'the highest point of all philosophy' (mandosio2012:567-568; farmer1998:7252). The editors of the Cambridge Oration record Farmer's correction of the numeral in their commentary (borghesi2012:4531-4537).
historiography: Farmer uses the pair 9>3-4 against Yates's claim that Pico's magic prepared operational attitudes to nature that led to modern science (farmer1998:7262-7270). The operative side of Pico's magic, he argues, is best read in terms of cosmic fall and redemption, so that the magus functions as a cosmic priest (farmer1998:7280-7289; farmer1998:7347). Mandosio states the general principle behind the thesis as 3>46 (mandosio2012:563-566). The thesis shows Pico building a claim about magic from a thesis in natural philosophy, and it preserves, through its wrong numeral, a trace of the censorship he imposed on his own text in press (editorial inference from farmer1998:25175-25178 and farmer1998:23416-23421).

quotations.text: our obligation to operate magic in the world

not_established: The text of the paradoxical thesis dropped before publication, which would restore Pico's numbering: not established by the sources consulted.

Why the thesis was dropped: Farmer judges that it was removed 'almost surely for theological reasons' (farmer1998:1487; borghesi2012:4537), but the thesis itself is not recovered in the sources consulted.
